title: The Storm Bell
text:
The wind had been rising all afternoon. By the time Ada finished her chores, it was hurling rain against the cottage windows like handfuls of gravel, and the sea beyond the harbour wall had turned the colour of wet slate.

Ada's grandmother sat by the stove, mending a net. "Your grandad's boat should be home by now," she said, without looking up. Her fingers, which never usually paused, had stopped moving.

Ada pressed her face to the glass. Out past the rocks, where the waves were breaking in great white fans, she thought she saw a light. It flickered, vanished, and then flickered again.

"Gran, there's a boat out there. It's heading for the Teeth!"

The Teeth were a row of jagged rocks at the mouth of the bay. Every child on the island knew the stories of the ships they had swallowed. In the old days, someone had always rung the storm bell on the cliff to warn sailors away, but nobody had climbed up to the bell tower for years.

Before her grandmother could stop her, Ada had pulled on her boots and was out of the door. The wind snatched her breath away. She bent almost double and scrambled up the cliff path, clinging to tufts of grass whenever her feet slipped on the mud.

The bell tower was little more than a stone hut with a rusty bell hanging from a beam. Ada grabbed the frayed rope and pulled with all her strength. Nothing happened. She pulled again, leaning back until she was almost sitting on the floor, and at last the bell gave a deep, groaning clang.

Again and again she rang it, until her arms burned and her palms were raw. Far below, the little light swung away from the rocks and began to creep slowly along the safe channel towards the harbour.

When Ada finally staggered home, her grandad was standing in the kitchen, dripping seawater onto the floor. He didn't say a word. He simply wrapped her in a hug that smelt of salt and diesel, and held on for a very long time.

title: Hedgehogs in Our Gardens
text:
Hedgehogs are one of Britain's best-loved wild animals, yet many people have never seen one. That is because hedgehogs are nocturnal: they sleep during the day and come out at dusk to search for food.

What do hedgehogs look like?
An adult hedgehog is about 25 centimetres long and is covered in around 5,000 to 7,000 spines. Each spine is a hollow, stiffened hair. When a hedgehog is frightened, it rolls into a tight ball, so that its soft face and belly are hidden and only the sharp spines point outwards.

What do they eat?
Despite their name, hedgehogs do not eat hedges! They are insectivores, which means that most of their diet is made up of insects and other small creatures. Beetles, caterpillars, earwigs and earthworms are among their favourite foods. A hungry hedgehog can travel up to two kilometres in a single night while it searches for a meal.

How do they survive the winter?
When food becomes hard to find in late autumn, hedgehogs hibernate. They build a nest of dry leaves under a hedge, a shed or a pile of logs, and their body temperature drops dramatically so that they use very little energy. Most hedgehogs sleep from around November until March, although they may wake up and move to a new nest once or twice.

Why do hedgehogs need our help?
Sadly, the number of hedgehogs in the countryside has fallen sharply in recent years. Many of their old homes, such as hedgerows and rough grassland, have disappeared, and busy roads are a serious danger to them.

How can you help?
• Make a "hedgehog highway" by cutting a hole about 13 centimetres square at the bottom of your garden fence, so that hedgehogs can travel between gardens.
• Leave a corner of your garden wild, with long grass and a pile of leaves.
• Put out a shallow dish of fresh water. Never give hedgehogs milk, because it can make them very ill.
• Check bonfires and long grass carefully before you light or cut them.

With a little care, every garden can become a safe stop on a hedgehog's night-time journey.

title: The Night Train
text:
At ten o'clock the platform sighs,
the clock above it blinks its eyes,
and out of darkness, long and low,
the night train rumbles, steady, slow.

Its windows glow like rows of moons,
its whistle hums forgotten tunes;
it stops to breathe a cloud of steam,
then gathers up the town's last dream.

A sleepy man with an umbrella,
a girl who hugs a shining cello,
a grandmother with knitting bag,
a puppy with a paper tag.

They climb aboard and find their seats,
they leave behind the empty streets,
and as the doors slide shut, they hear
the guard's long whistle, sharp and clear.

Clickety-clack, the wheels begin,
clickety-clack, the world spins in:
the sleeping fields, the silver mill,
the lonely farmhouse on the hill.

Through tunnels black as ink it flies,
past rivers holding starry skies,
past towns where every curtain's drawn
and no one's thinking yet of dawn.

The puppy dreams of chasing hares,
the sleepy man forgets his cares,
the grandmother has dropped a stitch,
the cello hums at every switch.

And when the eastern sky turns grey,
the night train slows and finds its way
out of the miles of dark it crossed,
and not a passenger is lost.

It sighs again, it settles down
beside some new, still-sleeping town,
and every traveller steps out new,
with morning shining through and through.

So if you wake at ten o'clock
and hear a rumble, hear a knock,
then close your eyes and count to three:
the night train waits for you and me.

title: The Journey of a Raindrop
text:
Have you ever wondered where rain comes from, or where a puddle goes when it disappears? The answer is the water cycle: a journey that the Earth's water has been making, over and over again, for billions of years. The water in your glass today may once have been drunk by a dinosaur!

Step 1: Evaporation
The journey begins when the Sun warms the water in seas, lakes and rivers. As the water heats up, some of it turns into an invisible gas called water vapour. This process is called evaporation. Water vapour also rises from the leaves of plants, and even from wet washing hanging on a line.

Step 2: Condensation
As the water vapour rises, it cools down. High in the sky the air is much colder, and the vapour turns back into tiny droplets of liquid water. This is called condensation. Billions of these droplets gather together to form clouds. You can see condensation at home, too: just look at the misty droplets that appear on a cold bathroom mirror after a hot shower.

Step 3: Precipitation
Inside a cloud, the droplets bump into each other and join together. Gradually they grow larger and heavier, until the air can no longer hold them up and they fall back to the ground. Any water that falls from the sky is called precipitation. It is often rain, but if the air is cold enough, it can also be sleet, hail or snow.

Step 4: Collection
When precipitation reaches the ground, it collects in rivers, lakes, oceans and underground. Some of it soaks into the soil, where it is taken up by the roots of plants. Much of it flows downhill in streams and rivers until it reaches the sea. There, the Sun warms it once more, and the whole cycle begins again.

The water cycle never stops. It moves water around our planet, fills our rivers and reservoirs, and keeps every living thing supplied with the water it needs to survive.
